When V exceeds √gh, the system consists only of ________ waves, there being no ________ waves or cusps. The two straight lines themselves are the front crests of the _________ system, and the ______ crests are _______ to the line of advance instead of _______ as in deep water.
opts: Diverging / transverse / diverging / inner / concave / convex
Diverging / transverse / diverging / outer / concave / convex
Diverging / transverse / diverging / inner / convex / concave
Transverse / diverging / transverse / outer / convex / concave
Transverse / diverging / transverse / inner / concave / convex

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988):

The wave-making resistance of a ship is the _____  fore-and-aft force upon the ship due to the fluid pressures acting ______  on all parts of the hull.
opts: Net / normally
Gross / normally
Net / parallel
Gross / parallel
Net / normally and parallel

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the wave-making resistance depends in large measure on:
opts: The shapes adopted for the area curve, waterlines and appendages.
The shapes adopted for the hull, bulbs if any and transverse sections.
The shapes adopted for the area curve, waterlines and transverse sections.
The shapes adopted for the area curve, waterlines and longitudinal sections.
The shapes adopted for the waterlines, longitudinal and transverse sections.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), at present, the most important tool available for reducing the resistance of specific ship designs is:
opts: Theoretical research
Model tests
Wind tunnels
Computer simulation
Full scale trials

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), regarding the total resistance coefficient curve of a ship, identify the alternative that correctly fills in the blanks:

At first the value of CT ________ with increase of speed. With further increase in speed, the value of CT begins to _______ more and more rapidly.
opts: Decreases / decrease
Decreases / increase
Increases / decrease
Increases / increase
Remains constant / increase

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), regarding the total resistance coefficient curve of a ship, at first the value of CT decreases with increase of speed. With further increase in speed, the value of CT begins to increase more and more rapidly, and up to the moment that the resistance may be varying at a power of V of 6 or more. This happens when the Froude number is approaching:

According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), regarding the total resistance coefficient curve of a ship, at first the value of CT decreases with increase of speed. With further increase in speed, the value of CT begins to increase more and more rapidly, and at Froude numbers approaching 0.45 the resistance may vary at a power of V of:
opts: 2 or more
4 or more
6 or more

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), Wigley (1931) investigated the effects of mutual wave interference upon wave-making resistance. He used a double-wedge-shaped body with parallel inserted in the middle, and found a symmetrical disturbance of the surface. About this term of the wave profile, identify the correct statements:

I) It has a peak at bow and stern and a trough along the center.
II) It dies out approximately two ship lengths astern of the hull.
III) It travels with the hull absorbing energy.
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
Only I is true
explanation: PNA Volume II pg. 22 (II- quickly ahead and astern of the hull / III- does not absorb any energy at constant speed)

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the results of mathematical research have been most valuable in providing an insight into the effects of mutual wave interference upon wave-making resistance. A most interesting example is that of a double-wedge-shaped body with parallel inserted in the middle, investigated by Wigley (1931). He showed that the expression for the wave profile along the hull contained:

I) A wave system at the bow, beginning with a crest.
II) A wave system at the forward shoulder, starting with a trough.
III) A wave system at the after shoulder, starting with a crest.
IV) A wave system at the stern, starting with a trough.
opts: All are true
Only I, II and IV are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and IV are true
Only I is true
explanation: PNA Volume II pg. 22-23 (III- trough / IV - crest)

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the task of the naval architect is to ensure that, within the limits of other design requirements, the hull form and propulsion arrangement will be the most efficient in the hydrodynamic sense. The ultimate test is that:

The ship shall perform at the required speed with the ________ of shaft power, and the problem is to attain the best combination of _______________.
opts: Minimum / hull and maneuvering.
Minimum / low resistance and high propulsive efficiency.
Maximum / low resistance and high propulsive efficiency.
Maximum / hull and maneuvering.
Maximum / hull and appendages.

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988):

I) A factor that influences the hydrodynamic design of a ship is the need to ensure not only good smooth-water performance but also that under average service conditions at sea the ship shall not suffer from any motions, wetness of decks, or lose speed in bad weather.
II) In general, we can assume that a hull form that is optimum in calm water will also be optimum in rough seas.
III) Recent research progress in oceanography and the seakeeping qualities of ships has made it possible to predict the relative performance of designs of varying hull proportions and form under different realistic sea conditions, using both model test and computing techniques.
opts: Only I and II are true
Only I is true
Only II is true
Only III is true
All are false
explanation: PNA Volume II pg. 1 (I- suffer from excessive... more than necessary /II- is not necessarily valid)

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), a consideration in powering of ships is the effect of:

I) Deterioration in hull surface condition in service as the result of fouling. 
II) Deterioration in hull surface condition in service as the result of corrosion. 
III) Propeller roughness on resistance and propulsion.
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
Only I is true

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in general, the basic contractual obligation laid on the shipbuilder is that the ship shall:
opts: Achieve a certain speed with a specified power in a trial on the sea route on which the ship is designed to operate, in the average weather conditions of regular operation.

Achieve a certain speed with a specified power in a trial in good weather on the sea route on which the ship is designed to operate, and for this reason smooth water performance is of great importance.
Achieve a certain speed with a specified power in average weather on trial, and for this reason good sea keeping ability is of great importance.
Achieve a certain speed with a specified power in good and bad weather on trials, and for this there should be a proper matching of hull and propeller.
Achieve a certain speed with a specified power in good weather on trial, and for this reason smooth water performance is of great importance.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the effect of sea condition is customarily allowed for by the provision of a service margin above the power required in smooth water. The determination of this service allowance depends on:
opts: Classification Societies minimum requirements.
Contractual values defined.
Simulation with computing techniques.
Tests with models in towing tanks.
The accumulation of sea-performance data on similar ships in similar trades.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), to deal with the total resistance of a ship more simply, it is usual to consider the total calm water resistance as being made up of four main components, which are:
opts: Frictional resistance, wave-making resistance, eddy resistance and air resistance.
Viscous resistance, wave-making resistance, eddy resistance and air resistance.
Frictional resistance, wave-making resistance, eddy resistance and appendage resistance.
Viscous resistance, wave-making resistance, eddy resistance and appendage resistance.
Frictional resistance, wave-making resistance, eddy resistance and form resistance.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), it is usual to consider the total calm water resistance as being made up of four main components. One of them is:
opts: The frictional and viscous resistance, due to the motion of the hull through a potential flow.
The frictional resistance, due to the motion of the hull through a viscous fluid.
The frictional resistance, due to the motion of the hull through a potential flow.
The viscous resistance, due to the motion of the hull through a frictional fluid.
The viscous resistance, due to the motion of the hull through a potential flow.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), it is usual to consider the total calm water resistance as being made up of four main components. One of them is:
opts: The wave-breaking resistance, due to the energy expended in diffracting waves caused by wind.
The wave-breaking resistance, due to the energy that must be supplied continuously by the ship to the wave system created on the surface of the water.
The wave-making resistance, due to the energy expended in diffracting waves caused by wind.
The wave-making resistance, due to the energy that must be supplied continuously by the ship to the wave system created on the surface of the water.
The wave-making resistance, due to the motions caused by waves, which subtracts and appreciable amount of energy and add to the resistance.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), it is usual to consider the total calm water resistance as being made up of four main components. One of them is:
opts: The eddy resistance, due to flow separation astern of the hull.
The eddy resistance, due to the energy carried away by eddies shed from the hull or appendages.
The eddy resistance, due to the energy supplied by eddies near the hull or appendages.
The eddy resistance, due to the motion of the hull through a viscous fluid.
The eddy resistance, due to the turbulent flow around the hull.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), it is usual to consider the total calm water resistance as being made up of four main components. One of them is:
opts: The air resistance experienced by the above-water part of the main hull and the superstructures due to the motion of the ship through the air.
The air resistance experienced by the above-water part of the main hull and the superstructures because of wind resistance to ahead motion.
The wind and air resistance experienced by the above-water part of the main hull and the superstructures due to the motion of the ship in open areas.
The wind resistance experienced by the above-water part of the main hull and the superstructures due to the motion of the ship through the air.
The wind resistance experienced by the above-water part of the main hull and the superstructures because of air resistance to ahead motion.

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988):

I) The importance of the different components of resistance depends upon the particular conditions of design, and much of the skill of naval architects lies in their ability to choose the shape and proportions of hull which will result in a combination leading to the minimum total power, compatible with other design constraints.
II) It is virtually impossible to discuss the various types of ship resistance without reference to model work.
III) A streamlined body moving in a straight horizontal line at constant speed, deeply immersed in an unlimited ocean, presents the simplest case of resistance.
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
Only I is true

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a streamlined body moving in a straight horizontal line at constant speed, deeply immersed in an unlimited ocean without viscosity:
opts: The velocity distribution past the hull, by Bernoulli´s Law, will be the inverse of the pressure distribution.
The velocity distribution past the hull, by d´Alembert´s principle, will be equal to the dynamic pressure distribution.
The velocity distribution past the hull, by Bernoulli´s Law, will be equal to the pressure distribution.
The velocity distribution past the hull, by d´Alembert´s principle, will be the inverse of the pressure distribution.
The velocity distribution past the hull, by Bernoulli´s Law, will be the inverse of the dynamic pressure distribution.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a fluid without viscosity, the pressure forces acting on a streamlined body moving deeply submerged in a straight horizontal line at constant speed will be:
opts: Absent.
Normal near the nose and stern and parallel to the hull at the middle body.
Parallel near the nose and stern and normal to the hull at the middle body.
Everywhere normal to the hull.
Everywhere parallel to the hull.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a fluid without viscosity, the pressure forces acting on a streamlined body moving deeply submerged in a straight horizontal line at constant speed result on forces that are:
opts: Equal on the fore and after bodies, so the body experiences no resistance.
Equal on the fore and after bodies, so the body experiences only pressure resistance.
Equal on the fore and after bodies, so the body experiences only wave-making resistance.
Higher at the fore body than at the after body, so there is a resistance to motion.
Higher at the aft body than at the fore body, so there is an assistance to motion.

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a real fluid the boundary layer alters:

I) The virtual shape of the stern.
II) The virtual length of the stern.
III) The pressure distribution.
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
Only I is true

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a real fluid the boundary layer alters the pressure distribution around a body moving in a straight horizontal line at constant speed in such a way that:
opts: The sternward components at the stern are reduced and the forward components at the forward portion of the body are little changed from that in a perfect fluid.
The sternward components at the stern are reduced and the components at the forward portion of the body are little changed from that in a perfect fluid.
The sternward components at the stern are increased and the components at the forward portion of the body are little changed from that in a perfect fluid.
The forward components at the stern are reduced and the components at the forward portion of the body are little changed from that in a perfect fluid.
The forward components at the stern are increased and the components at the forward portion of the body are little changed from that in a perfect fluid.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), a body moving in a real fluid:
opts: May experience frictional resistance or eddy resistance depending on the Reynolds number of the flow.
May experience frictional resistance or eddy resistance depending on the Froude number of the flow.
Experiences frictional resistance and perhaps eddy resistance also.
Experiences eddy resistance and perhaps frictional resistance also.
Always experiences frictional resistance and eddy resistance.

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a body moving in a real fluid:

The fluid immediately in contact with the surface of the body is carried ______ the surface, and that in the close vicinity is set in motion in the _____ direction as that in which the body is moving.
opts: Along with / opposite
Away from / opposite
Along with / same
Away from / same
Along and away from / opposite

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a real fluid, a body experiences a layer of water, which gets gradually thicker from the bow to the stern, and in which the velocity varies from that of the body at its surface to that appropriate to the potential flow pattern at the outer edge of the layer. This layer is called the boundary layer, and the momentum supplied to the water in it by the hull is a measure of the:
opts: Eddy resistance
Form resistance
Frictional resistance
Residuary resistance
Viscous resistance

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), a body moving in a straight horizontal line at constant speed in a real fluid leaves a frictional wake:
opts: Behind it in the same direction as the body.
Ahead of it in the opposite direction as the potential flow.
Behind it in the opposite direction as the body.
Ahead of it in the same direction as the body.
Behind it in the same direction as the potential flow.

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), a body moving in a straight horizontal line at constant speed in a real fluid leaves a frictional wake that:

I) Can be detected far astern of the body.
II) Represents a continual drain of energy.
III) Can be used in studies to measure the frictional drag.
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
All are false

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a body moving in a real fluid:

If the body is rather blunt at the after end, the flow may leave the form at some point, thus ________ the total pressure on the __________ and adding to the resistance.
opts: Increasing / afterbody
Increasing / middle body
Reducing / afterbody
Reducing / forebody
Reducing / middle body

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the movement of the hull on the surface of the sea creates a pressure distribution of:
opts: Decreased pressure at the bow and stern, and of increased pressure over the middle part of the length.
Decreased pressure at the bow, and of increased pressure over the stern and middle part of the length.
Increased pressure at the bow and middle part of the length, and of decreased pressure over the stern.
Increased pressure at the bow and stern, and of decreased pressure over the middle part of the length.
Increased pressure at the bow, and of decreased pressure over the stern and middle part of the length.

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988):

I) The resulting added resistance due to wave-making corresponds to the drain of energy into the wave system, which spreads out astern of the ship and has to be continuously recreated.
II) The presence of the wave systems modifies the skin friction and other resistances.
III) There is a very complicated interaction among all the different components of resistance.
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
All are false

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988):

One has only to look down from the deck of a ship at sea and observe the ________ motion in the water near the hull, increasing in extent from bow to stern, to realize that energy is being absorbed in _________ resistance.
opts: Laminar / eddy
Laminar / frictional
Turbulent / eddy
Turbulent / frictional
Turbulent / separation

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the turbulent motion in the water near the hull, increasing in extent from bow to stern, results in energy being absorbed in frictional resistance. Experiments have shown that even in smooth, new slow-speed ships, the residuary resistance can represent up to:
opts: 10% of the total resistance
15% of the total resistance
20% of the total resistance
25% of the total resistance
30% of the total resistance

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the turbulent motion in the water near the hull, increasing in extent from bow to stern, results in energy being absorbed in frictional resistance. Experiments have shown that in smooth, new slow-speed ships, the residuary resistance can represent at least:
opts: 5% of the total resistance
10% of the total resistance
15% of the total resistance
20% of the total resistance
25% of the total resistance

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988):

I) Froude concluded that the model-ship extrapolation problem could only be solved by dividing the resistance into two components.
II) Froude found that at any given speed the resistance was less for a long plank than for a shorter one.
III) Froude gave an empirical formula for the resistance in the form R = fSV^n
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
Only III is true
explanation: PNA Volume II pg. 7 (II- specific resistance per unit of surface area)

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988):

I) Experiments have shown that even in smooth new ships, the frictional resistance accounts for 80 to 85 percent of the viscous resistance in slow-speed ships and as much as 50 percent in high-speed ships.
II) Any roughness of the surface will increase the frictional resistance appreciably over that of smooth surface, and with subsequent corrosion and fouling still greater increases will occur.
III) Not only does the nature of the surface affect the drag, but the wake and propulsive performance are also changed.
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
Only I is true
explanation: PNA Volume II pg. 7 (I- of the total resistance)

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), Froude found that at any given speed the specific resistance per unit of surface area was less for a long plank than for a shorter one, which he attributed to the fact that:
opts: Towards the after end of the long plank the water had acquired a sternward motion and so had a lower relative velocity.
Towards the after end of the short plank the water had acquired a forward motion and so had a lower relative velocity.
Towards the after end of the short plank the water had acquired a sternward motion and so had a lower absolute velocity.
Towards the after end of the long plank the water had acquired a forward motion and so had a lower relative velocity.
Towards the after end of the long plank the water had acquired a forward motion and so had a lower absolute velocity.

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in order to apply the results to ships, the derived skin-friction coefficients had to be extrapolated to much greater lengths and speeds. W. Froude did not give these extrapolated figures in his reports, but suggested two methods which might be used for their derivation. In his own words:

It is once seen that, at a length of 50 feet, the _______, with increasing length, of the friction per square foot of every additional length is so ______ that it will make ________ difference in our estimate of the total resistance of a surface 300 ft long whether we assume such a ________ to continue at the same rate through the last 250 feet of surface, or to cease entirely after 50 feet; while it is perfectly certain that the truth must lie somewhere between these assumptions.
opts: Decrease / high / a considerable / decrease
Decrease / high / no very great / increase
Decrease / small / no very great / decrease
Increase / high / a considerable / increase
Increase / small / no very great / increase

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), Froude also obtained some full-scale information in an attempt to confirm his law of comparison and to assist in the extrapolation of the frictional coefficients to ship lengths by carrying out towing tests on the sloop HMS Greyhound, a wooden ship with copper sheating over the bottom.

The actual ship resistance was everywhere _____ than the predicted from the model, the percentage ______ becoming ______ with increasing speed.
opts: Lower / decrease / less
Lower / decrease / higher
Higher / increase / less
Higher / increase / higher
Higher / decrease / higher

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), Froude also obtained some full-scale information in an attempt to confirm his law of comparison and to assist in the extrapolation of the frictional coefficients to ship lengths by carrying out towing tests on the sloop HMS Greyhound, a wooden ship with copper sheating over the bottom. The actual ship resistance was everywhere higher than the predicted from the model, the percentage increase becoming less with increasing speed.

The difference in R/V2, however, is almost the same at all speeds, except the _______, and _______ only slowly with _______ speed, as might occur if this additional resistance were of viscous type and varying at some power less than the second.
opts: Lowest / decreases / increasing
Highest / decreases / increasing
Highest / increases / decreasing
Lowest / increases / increasing
Highest / increases / increasing

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in his paper on the Greyhound trials, Froude states quite clearly how he applied his idea of the “equivalent plank” resistance. For this calculation the immersed skin was carefully measured, and the resistance due to it determined upon the hypothesis that it is equivalent to that of a rectangular surface of:
opts: Equal area of the model, moving at corresponding speeds.
Equal area, and length (in the line of motion) equal to that of the model, moving at the same speed.
Equal area, length and breadth of the model, moving at corresponding speeds.
Equal area, length and breadth of the model, moving at the same speed.
Equal length of the model, moving at corresponding speeds.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), Osbourne Reynolds made water flow through a glass tube, introducing a thin stream of dye on the centerline at the entrance of the tube. Below the critical velocity, in this case, the resistance to flow in the pipe varied:
opts: Inversely with the speed
At the square root of the speed
Directly as the speed
At a power of the speed around 1.5
At a power of the speed somewhat less than 2

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), Osbourne Reynolds made water flow through a glass tube, introducing a thin stream of dye on the centerline at the entrance of the tube. Above the critical velocity, the resistance to flow in the pipe varied:
opts: Inversely with the speed
At the square root of the speed
Directly as the speed
At a power of the speed around 1.5
At a power of the speed somewhat less than 2

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), experiments such as those performed by Reynolds suggested that there were:
opts: Only one flow regime possible, although associated with two different resistance laws.
Two separate flow regimes possible, each associated with a different resistance law.
Two separate flow regimes possible, although associated with the same resistance law.
Four separate flow regimes possible, each associated with a different resistance law.
Four separate flow regimes possible, although associated with the same resistance law.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), when a dye filament retains its own identity and the fluid flows in layers which do not mix transversely, but slide over one another at relative speeds which varies across the pipe section, the flow is called:
opts: Laminar and is associated with a relatively low resistance.
Turbulent and is associated with a relatively low resistance.
Laminar and is associated with a relatively high resistance.
Turbulent and is associated with a relatively high resistance.
Viscous and is associated with a relatively high resistance.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), experiments as those performed by Reynolds suggested that there were two separate flow regimes possible, each associated with a different resistance law. In accordance with those findings, when the velocity is increased the Rn is:
opts: Increased
Decreased
First increases and then decreases
First decreases and then increases
Remains constant

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), experiments as those performed by Reynolds suggested that there were two separate flow regimes possible, each associated with a different resistance law. In accordance with those findings, when the diameter (or length/size) is increased, the Rn is:
opts: Increased
Decreased
First increases and then decreases
First decreases and then increases
Remains constant

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in modern skin-friction formulations the specific frictional resistance coefficient is assumed to be a function of:

I) Reynolds number
II) Froude number
III) Weber number
opts: All are true
Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only I is true
Only II is true

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in a plank, Blasius found that laminar flow became unstable at Reynolds number of the order of:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), as the speed of the flow is increased, the transition from laminar flow to turbulent flow:
opts: Occurs simultaneously over the whole plank.
Occurs first at the inboard side of the plank and later at the outboard side of the plank.
Occurs first at the outboard side of the plank and later at the inboard side of the plank.
Occurs first at the upstream part of the plank and later at the downstream part of the plank.
Occurs first at the downstream part of the plank and later at the upstream part of the plank.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the transition from laminar flow to turbulent flow does not occur simultaneously over the whole plank. For the constant value of the local Rn at which transition takes place:
opts: The distance from the leading edge will decrease as the velocity increases.
The distance from the leading edge will increase as the velocity increases.
The distance from the trailing edge will decrease as the velocity increases.
The distance from the trailing edge will not change as the velocity increases.
The distance from the trailing edge will increase as velocity increases while the flow is laminar, passing to decrease when the flow becomes turbulent.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the transition from laminar flow to turbulent flow does not occur simultaneously over the whole plank. In this transition:
opts: The value of the frictional coefficient will decrease along a transition line and finally approach the turbulent line asymptotically.
The value of the frictional coefficient will increase along a transition line and finally approach the turbulent line asymptotically.
The value of the frictional coefficient will decrease along a transition line and finally approach the turbulent line abruptly as the eddy motion disrupts the different layers of laminar flow.
The value of the frictional coefficient will increase along a transition line and finally approach the turbulent line abruptly as the eddy motion disrupts the different layers of laminar flow.
The value of the frictional coefficient will decrease along a transition line and finally approach the turbulent line at an increasingly rate up to stabilize itself asymptotically.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in 1935 the ICSTS agreed to adopt the Froude method of model extrapolation, establishing that for every kind of vessel the length to be used is:
opts: Length at 70% of the depth
Length at the main deck
Length between perpendiculars
Length on the water line
Length overall

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in 1935 the ICSTS agreed to adopt the Froude method of model extrapolation, establishing that the wetted surface is adopted as:
opts: The maximum beam multiplied by the length.
The mean draft multiplied by the length.
The mean girth multiplied by the length.
The maximum girth multiplied by the length.
The mean beam multiplied by the length.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in 1935 the ICSTS agreed to adopt the Froude method of model extrapolation, establishing that all model results should be corrected to a standard temperature of:
opts: 10 deg C
15 deg C
20 deg C
25 deg C
30 deg C

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), Hughes, in association with his two-dimensional line, proposed a new method of extrapolation from model to ship. He assumed that the total model resistance coefficient could be divided into:
opts: Two parts, representing the viscous resistance and the wave-making resistance.
Two parts, representing the frictional resistance and the wave-making resistance.
Two parts, representing the frictional resistance and the form resistance.
Three parts, representing the viscous resistance, the form resistance and the wave-making resistance.
Three parts, representing the frictional resistance, the form resistance and the residuary resistance.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), before the run-in point, the value of the total resistance coefficient can be identified as being the:
opts: Eddy-making resistance coefficient
Total form resistance coefficient
Total frictional resistance coefficient
Total viscous resistance coefficient
Wave-making resistance coefficient

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), the form factor (1+k) is assumed to:
opts: Vary linearly with Rn
Be inversely proportional to Rn
Vary linearly with Fn
Be inversely proportional to Fn
Be invariant with Rn

q:
According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), regarding the methods of extrapolation of model results to ships:

In the ________ method the whole of the model residuary resistance coefficient is transferred to the ship unchanged, while in the _______ method only that part of the residuary resistance coefficient attributed to _______ effects is reduced in the transfer.
opts: Form factor / Froude / friction
Form factor / Froude / viscous
Froude / form factor / form
Froude / form factor / friction
Froude / form factor / viscous

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in the case of the form factor method for extrapolation of model results to ships:
opts: The slope and vertical position of the two-dimensional friction line matters.
Only the slope of the three-dimensional friction line matters.
Only the slope of the two-dimensional friction line matters.
Only the vertical position of the three-dimensional friction line matters.
Only the vertical position of the two-dimensional friction line matters.

q: According to Principles of Naval Architecture (1988), in the case of the Froude method for extrapolation of model results to ships:
opts: Only the slope and vertical position of the two-dimensional friction line matters.
